a.title:
VR Cinematics
for UE 5.8
a.subtitle: Record it in VR. Re-shoot it from anywhere. Render it once.
a.thesis: A VR recording is a set, not a finished film. Measure its problems, fix them with three ideas, and put new cameras in it.
a.takeaway: A recording is a set. Put a new camera in it.
a.cover_spoken: Welcome. Alex teaches live, 10:00–12:00 ET. We will use recorded video first; each optional live demo has a machine and a click path. Ask questions in chat. The two breaks are 10:45 and 11:25 ET. The two-hour class keeps the core ACCVR video segment; extended camera history remains in Talk B.

b.title:
How We Built the Cameras
for A Christmas Carol VR
b.subtitle: From a spacebar to a cinematographer build

pool.title:
Raw VR
Footage
Looks Bad.
pool.tagline: Four problems, and one take we can measure.
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 10:03–10:04 ET. Part one is why you can't just publish what a headset records.

CLASS CLOCK: 10:04–10:06 ET. Four problems. Shake: tracking noise and hand tremor at 72 to 120 Hz. Tilt: head roll tips the horizon, and roll can make a flat-screen recording uncomfortable. Jump: teleports and snap turns are instant cuts the viewer never chose. FOV: the headset sees about 100 degrees and a 16:9 screen does not, so the framing was never meant for a flat frame. Hold the four words on screen and ask the chat which one they notice most in their own captures.

pool.alt: Side by side: the recorded head camera on the left, jittery with a tilted horizon, and the stabilized camera on the right, steady and level. The same twenty-second take.
pool.credit: Class practice take · jitter 1.54 to 0.18 deg RMS · VR Cinematics kit
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 10:08–10:09 ET. Same comparison in motion, twenty seconds, looped. Watch the horizon on the left. This take is a seeded practice take built to have the same problems as a real recording, so every student has the identical numbers.

CLASS CLOCK: 10:09–10:10 ET. Measured, not eyeballed. On the class practice take: jitter is the RMS of what a 0.05 second Gaussian would remove, 1.54 degrees before and 0.18 after. Angular acceleration is the seasick number: 2575 degrees per second squared before, 136 after. Residual roll goes from 13.3 degrees to zero. Everyone will run the measure tool on their own copy and should see the same dialog. These numbers are from the seeded 20 second take at 90 Hz, verified on UE 5.8.2.

pool.title:
Stabilize
It.
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 10:50–10:51 ET. Part three. Do it by hand once so the one-click version is not magic.

CLASS CLOCK: 10:51–10:54 ET. Idea one. Don't filter three Euler curves. They break near yaw 180 and at steep pitch, which is exactly where players look. Convert to quaternions, flip signs so neighbors agree, because q and minus q are the same rotation and averaging across a sign flip collapses to zero. Filter the four components, renormalize, convert back, and unwrap yaw so keys never jump from 359 to 0, which Sequencer would render as a full spin. Use a zero-phase filter: offline there is no reason to accept lag, and a lagging POV turns after the player did.

pool.title:
Never Smooth
Across a Teleport
pool.subtitle: Idea two: segment first, then filter
pool.alt: A diagram: the true camera path jumps at a teleport; a filter run across the jump starts drifting about ten frames early, while a filter run on each segment does not.
bullets: Teleports and snap turns move faster than any head can: over 8 m/s or 1000 °/s
A 45° snap turn at 90 Hz is about 4000 °/s
Smooth each segment on its own, then cut on the jump: a cut hides it for free
Measured on the class take: over 30 cm off the true path 10 frames early, versus under 3 cm segmented
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 10:54–10:57 ET. Idea two, and the one most students have never seen. If you run a filter across a teleport, the camera starts drifting toward the destination about ten frames before the jump: a swoop through the set. On the class take it was more than 30 centimeters off the true path ten frames early, against under 3 centimeters when each segment is filtered separately. The class tool finds discontinuities with thresholds of 8 meters per second and 1000 degrees per second. Then it marks them with TAKE CUT markers, and you cut on those frames. Never cut anywhere else.

pool.bigText:
Level the horizon.
Nobody misses the roll.
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 10:57–10:59 ET. Idea three. Scale the residual roll toward zero. Roll can make a flat recording uncomfortable in head-camera footage and viewers do not miss it. On the class take it goes from 13.3 degrees to zero. One caution: a head-centered path from an avatar head bone needs about 14 centimeters of forward offset, or the POV renders from inside the head mesh. Take Recorder's HMD camera is already at the eyes.

pool.bigText:
By hand:
Curve Editor → Filter Tool
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 10:59–11:04 ET. Students follow along here. Open the take's Camera or VR_Head transform curves in the Curve Editor, select the rotation channels, run the Euler filter first, then a Gaussian or an FFT low-pass. It works, per channel, and it is blind to teleports, which is why we then do the one-click version. Epic ships its own scripted version at Engine/Plugins/VirtualProduction/VirtualCamera/Content/Python/VCamSmooth.py: Bake plus Gaussian. LIVE OPTION: Lenovo — open the recorded Level Sequence, select the Camera transform channels, open Curve Editor > Filter Tool, duplicate before filtering, split at a teleport, then compare at that boundary.

pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:15–11:19 ET. Make it yours re-time the Camera Cuts track, swap a shot to another camera, add one hand-keyed camera move. The rule is simple: always cut at a TAKE CUT marker. Those are the frames where the player teleported or snap turned, and a cut hides that jump for free. Every student should leave with a cut that differs from yours.

pool.title: A Draft Is for Checking Angles
pool.subtitle: 1 Wide: establishes the room · 2 Medium: the instruction wall · 3 Close: crops the text, so reframe it before the final

items.t:
Real motion blur
from 90 Hz keys

pool.notes:
SAY: This clip isn't about beautiful shots. It proves the pipeline: a recorded take, three angles picked from the viewport, cut in Sequencer, rendered by Movie Render Queue as a draft.
SAY: Angle one is a wide establishing shot of the room, angle two is a medium on the instruction wall, and angle three is a close-up that crops the text badly.
SAY: That bad third angle is the point. The draft cost seconds, and it caught a framing mistake before an expensive final render.

CLASS CLOCK: 11:31–11:38 ET. Play the new 4.9-second MRQ draft and let it loop. It comes from the actual stock Take Recorder camera exercise in the UOXR take-home branch: record, scrub the saved take, choose three viewport angles, build the Sequencer cut, render 147 frames at 30 fps. This is scripted desktop camera motion, not a fresh XR head/hand recording. Point out the third angle crops the OPENXR header: inspect and reframe a draft before committing to a final. The original twenty-second seeded kit render remains the polished cold open. Draft is 720p; Final is 1080p with eight temporal samples. Render times depend on shader caches; use the prepared clip during class. The source-camera cut must not override a master edit, so the plugin preserves the source and creates a performance copy without its camera-cut track. The flat command-line route disables HMD and debug view modes; these are process-local settings. LIVE OPTION: Lenovo — launch the prepared desktop project with VRCineTools and Takes enabled and -nohmd, open /VRCineTools/Takes/ClassRecorded_01_PickedCut, inspect its three Camera Cuts, reframe PickedCam_03, then use Movie Render Queue with MRQ_Draft. Show Movie Render Graph as an alternate configuration path; no MRG render claim.

pool.title: The Three Render Traps
pool.subtitle: Every one exits cleanly and writes nothing useful
pool.alt: A contact sheet: three frames from each of the five camera rigs, each labeled with its rig and frame number.
bullets: Zero frames: the output frame rate is below the sequence rate
Empty file names: {sequence_name} expands to nothing on the legacy command-line path
Black frames: an untitled level, or no Camera Cuts track
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:38–11:41 ET. Three traps that all look like success. Zero frames: the output frame rate is below the sequence's. Empty file names: on the legacy command-line preset path in 5.8.2, the sequence name token resolves to an empty string and frames land in Saved/MovieRenders named .0000.png, so write the sequence name literally into the preset. Black frames: an untitled level cannot render, or the sequence has no Camera Cuts track, or every cut points at a missing camera. The contact sheet is the check: look at the start, middle and end frame of every shot before you trust a render.

pool.bigText:
Open the shutter
at the frame.
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:41–11:44 ET. A subtle one, for people rendering with temporal samples. The default shutter centers on the frame time, so on the first frame after a teleport or snap turn half the sub-samples see the old pose and half the new, and MRQ averages them into a see-through double exposure. Set MoviePipelineCameraSetting shutter_timing to FRAME_OPEN: the shutter opens at the frame and integrates forward, so a cut on the jump never ghosts. Verified on 5.8.2: frames on both sides of the snap turn and the teleport were clean single exposures, and real motion blur survived on a pan. In Movie Render Graph it is the camera node's ShutterTiming. Draft renders with one temporal sample can't show this, so check the final preset's shot-start frames.

pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:45–11:46 ET. Four generations of camera tooling on one show. 2023: MagicCam, a Blueprint that calls shot presets from the keyboard. December 2025, the final run: a livestream with a human cinematographer directing, and cameras generated procedurally for specific characters. Then the show recorded as data, so the camera is free after the fact. And in October 2026 a cinematographer build that lets visitors shoot new coverage of the recording and assemble a working cut. Each generation made the previous one's assumption obvious: a camera is a rig you place, then a shot you call, then a decision you can revisit. The 2023 stop is dated from the Blueprint's last-saved version (December 2023); earlier seasons had cameras too, and I did not document them. ALEX TO CONFIRM:

pool.title: MagicCam: A Shot Is a Struct
pool.subtitle: A Christmas Carol VR, 2023, Unreal Engine 5.2
pool.alt: A card showing a shot preset as a struct with height, distance, rotation, performers and MetaHuman sockets, and the keys that call presets.
bullets: Keys 0–9 and Alt+0–9 call SetCam0 to SetCam13; PageUp and PageDown cycle
Each preset is one struct: height, distance, rotation, who to look at, which sockets
Two-shot compositions: “Character A on Left, Character B on Right”
Height comes off a MetaHuman face socket, so the framing follows the performer
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:46–11:47 ET. The 2023 camera Blueprint is called BP_MagicCamera. 601 nodes. Keys 0 to 9 and Alt combinations call SetCam0 through SetCam13, and PageUp and PageDown cycle through them. Every preset calls one macro, CamSet, with a struct: a height offset, a distance, a rotation, which performer to look at, which performer to snap to, left and right axis sockets, a socket to look at, a socket to offset from, and a look-at offset. The sockets are MetaHuman face sockets such as FACIAL_C_NoseTip, which is how a camera framed for a short performer stays framed for a tall one. The comment on the macro says Character A on the left, Character B on the right: these are two-shot compositions. The lesson for your project: make the shot a data structure, and have the key press just select one. The struct field list is exact; the card's wording of each field is a paraphrase of the Blueprint's pin names. Read from Alex's pasted T3D export with the blueprint-reader, not from the live project.

pool.title: Damped Follow, and a Camera That Never Frames Nothing
pool.subtitle: The rest of MagicCam
pool.alt: The ghost of Jacob Marley in A Christmas Carol VR
bullets: Toggles for distance damping and look-at; a damping of zero is a hard cut
On a camera switch it waits 0.2 s, then snaps the damping to its target
Distance and height scale with the performer’s Z scale × 0.8
A hidden performer is swapped for an invisible “dummy Marley head”, so a camera never frames an empty spot
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:47–11:48 ET. Three details from the same Blueprint that are worth stealing. A damped follow with toggles for distance damping and look-at, where a damping value of zero is a hard cut. On a camera switch it waits 0.2 seconds and then sets the actual damping equal to the target, so the new shot doesn't glide in from the old one. Distance and height are scaled by the performer's Z scale times 0.8. And a hidden performer is swapped for an invisible dummy Marley head, so a preset that frames a character who is currently offstage still has something to frame. The 2026 notes list the same guard as a port worth making: jump and preset targets should skip hidden characters.

pool.title: Replay: Any Seat in the House
pool.alt: A recorded performance played back in the replay system: Marley’s ghost confronts Scrooge, seen from a free camera with the replay controls on screen.
pool.credit: Replay recording of a performance · A Christmas Carol VR · Yu-Jun Yeh
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:45–11:46 ET. Here is the replay system. We recorded the performances as data, using Unreal's replay recording of the live session: the motion capture, the cues and the spatial audio, not video. That means the camera is free after the fact. Scrub the timeline, fly anywhere, and see the controls on screen. Everything after this slide is about what it took to make a free camera in a replay actually reliable.

pool.title: Replay Playback Will Bite You
pool.subtitle: Four fixes from the 2026 camera build (UE 5.4)
pool.alt: A scene from A Christmas Carol VR
bullets: RepNotifies fire before BeginPlay on the first bunch: re-apply values at the end of BeginPlay
A replay viewer is a client, so live-session watchdogs run and eject you: gate them on “is playing replay”
Seek cooldown: time it from the completion callback, not the start
Pause by setting a world pauser: demo time and audio stop, the camera keeps flying
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:50–11:51 ET. Four things any project that plays back DemoNetDriver replays will hit; we found them in the 2024 project on UE 5.4. One: on the first bunch, RepNotifies run before BeginPlay, so anything BeginPlay creates, like a dynamic material or a widget, isn't there yet. The symptom was every avatar the same green with no name until you skipped once. Fix: re-apply the replicated values at the end of BeginPlay. Two: a replay viewer is a client, so a live-session watchdog that watches a server heartbeat stalls during a seek or a long pause, and then calls JoinSession and kicks you out of the replay. 'Pressing skip too fast crashes it' was really one seek. Fix: gate every reconnect on is-playing-replay. Three: don't start another seek until about 30 frames and three-quarters of a second after the previous seek's completion callback. Four: there is no demopause command in 5.4; setting any PlayerState as the world pauser stops demo time and sound while the spectator camera keeps flying. These are from our KB technique note and verified in PIE on the 2024 project; your engine version and project may differ.

pool.bigText:
A seek can bring back
a scene that's gone.
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:51–11:51 ET. A beautiful one. When we sought into a beat where Dickens's parlor had already vanished, the replay restored the streamed-out parlor for about four seconds and replayed its dissolve, in the middle of someone's shot. Our fix is unglamorous: a five second pre-roll under a black card. The cut starts, you see black, the world settles, then the shot begins. In this show, seek restoration needed a settling interval. Check the scene after each seek; the five-second pre-roll is a project-specific workaround.

pool.title: The Title Card Is a Decision
pool.subtitle: What to call it, and who gets the credit
pool.alt: A black 2.39 title card: A CHRISTMAS CAROL VR, WORKING CUT with version and date, the scene, Shot by names, and Performed live by Ari Tarr and Debbie Deer, Work in progress.
bullets: “Director’s Cut” means the director’s own version: the wrong label
“Working cut” plus a version number is the honest one
Credit “Shot by”, not “DP”: visitors frame and cut, they don’t light
The version goes up per export, not per edit
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:53–11:53 ET. A small decision that took research and is worth showing, because it's the same thinking as naming a render. Editing stages run assembly, rough cut, fine cut, picture lock; an unfinished film shown to an audience is a work-in-progress screening; a delivery head slate carries the title, version, date and running time. Director's Cut would have claimed the director made it. For the credit: a DP sets the look and runs camera and lighting crews, a camera operator frames, an editor decides when to cut. Visitors frame, choose the lens, and choose the cuts, but light nothing, and many people don't know the abbreviation DP. So the on-screen credit is Shot by, followed by names. The card shown is the template; the fields in angle brackets are filled per cut. Decision record: 2026-10-22.

pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:53–11:54 ET. We wanted a phone-as-camera feel in the cut. Findings: UE 5.1 moved the VirtualCamera plugin to Runtime, but the 5.4 docs still call it the in-editor Virtual Camera system; Live Link in a packaged game needs the messaging flag and Shipping is unsupported; and an Epic staff reply on a 2024 forum thread confirmed that enabling a VCam actor crashes a packaged build because it loads editor-only code. So in the project, V toggles the level's VCam component, the cinematographer plugin reads it by reflection with no module dependency, and packaged builds are unaffected and use the normal camera. That is the 5.4.4 answer. ALEX TO CONFIRM: not re-tested on 5.8, which is what this class uses; check before telling students it works or doesn't.

pool.bigText:
Cameras are data.
Shots are structs.
Credit the operator.
pool.notes: CLASS CLOCK: 11:54–11:55 ET. The three things to take from five winters of cameras. Cameras are data: whether it's a Blueprint struct, a JSON file of shot slots, or a recorded replay, if the shot is data you can change your mind afterward. Shots are structs: the key press only selects. And credit the operator: the moment a visitor can make a shot, the title card and the credit become part of the design.
